name: Ben Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing mechanical engineering, so it's lectures on statics and materials, plus a CAD lab on Wednesdays that I actually love. I share a cold terraced house with three other students, and we split the heating very carefully. Saturdays and Sundays I'm behind the counter at a café near the station, and that pays for my food. Dad picks orders in a warehouse and can't send me anything, so the loan is basically it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was a useful tool that got overhyped, like a lot of things. At the café, the ordering app saves the manager ten minutes a week and nobody lost a job. I'd tell my flatmates not to panic about a robot coming for engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my plan stays the same: finish the degree, get a graduate engineering job in a firm that makes things. I'm not top of my year, so I'd still be competing for the same few places. And rent keeps going up. That worries me more than any machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and try to land a summer placement after second year, because I've heard that's how people actually get hired. I'd also ask the careers office to look at my CV, which is mostly café work. And I'd keep the weekend shifts, even if they tire me out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit flat. It's not frightening, but the money pressure is still sitting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent worries you more. What's the number you're looking at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I pay 420 a month, bills included, and my loan for living costs doesn't quite reach that. The café covers the gap, but if my hours dropped for a month I'd be borrowing from Dad, and he doesn't have it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your dad about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. He'd feel bad and skip something himself, so I'd rather cut my own food budget first.

say: AI was a **useful tool** that got overhyped, like a lot of things.
Nobody at my café lost a job when the ordering app arrived.
think: My plan stays the same, but I'm not top of my year, so **competition** for places stays tough.
Rising **rent** worries me more than any machine.
do: Look for a **summer placement** after second year.
Ask the careers office to improve my **CV**, which is mostly café work.
feel: A bit **flat**, since the money pressure sits there even without AI.
S0.quote: I pay 420 a month, bills included, and my loan for living costs doesn't quite reach that.
fieldNote: Money, not AI, is what sits on him in the quiet picture.
He would **hide** a shortfall from his dad rather than ask for help.
Mechanical work is less exposed, so his **calm** about the degree follows from his field.

steps.text: Keep the weekend café shifts all year
Apply for summer engineering placements before second year
Cut my own food budget before asking Dad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and it's going to change a lot of jobs, but engineering has time. Software will do more of the drawing and checking, so engineers who can use it will do better. I'd tell friends in computing and business to be careful because they're first in line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it affects me more than I show. If the checking and the drawing get automated, firms need fewer juniors, and I'm exactly the person who'd be junior. But hands-on engineering, like working in a plant or on site, changes slower, so I'd point myself there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the CAD software's AI features properly, not just now and then. I'd ask in my placement search for firms that actually make things, like machinery or energy, rather than office design. And I'd join the engineering society's AI workshop series on Thursdays, because it's free and has people from industry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit on edge, but not panicked. It feels like standing at a crossing and waiting for the lights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said juniors might get fewer jobs. Who do you think is responsible for helping with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly firms, because they should still train people, and partly government. I'd like rules that say big companies using AI must hire a number of apprentices or graduates. Left alone, they'll just cut the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if no placement came through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try a smaller firm, even for less money. Failing that, I'd take a technician job and do a part-time degree while working, because getting experience matters more than the title.

say: Engineers who can use the **new software** will do better.
Big firms should be required to keep hiring **apprentices** and graduates.
think: Fewer **junior** roles would hit me, since I'd be exactly that junior.
Hands-on work like a **plant** or a site changes slower, so I'd aim there.
do: Use the **AI features** in my CAD software properly, not just sometimes.
Target firms that **make things**, like machinery or energy.
feel: **On edge** but not panicked, like waiting at a crossing for the lights.
S1.quote: If the checking and the drawing get automated, firms need fewer juniors, and I'm exactly the person who'd be junior.
fieldNote: He sees engineering as **later** exposed than computing but still expects to feel it.
His answer points to **firms and government** together, fitting a progressive, rules-minded view.
He moves from tools to a concrete **placement plan**, showing steady adaptability.

steps.text: Learn the AI features in my CAD software
Target machinery and energy firms for placements
Join the engineering society's Thursday AI workshops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it needs an emergency response, because two years is not a transition, it's a shock. Governments should be talking about income support, and companies should have to share what they gain. I'd be loud about it at the students' union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. By 2028 I'd be in second year, and the whole idea of graduating into an engineering job could be gone. Hands-on robots come about 2031, so some of my field survives a bit longer, but the design and checking jobs go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the degree for now, because a qualification still matters and I need somewhere to be. I'd ask my lecturers what's actually safe in the field. I'd also save everything I can from the café, maybe taking a third shift, and I'd look at whether a technician route is cheaper than finishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly, and angry. I don't think it's fair that people my age wouldn't get a chance to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take a third shift. What does that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sleep and study time, mainly. I'd probably slip behind in the maths. But I'd rather have a bit of money in the bank than a perfect mark, if the jobs are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe job look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something physical that a robot can't do yet, like fixing machines on site. But that's only safe till about 2031, so it's a few years, not a career.

say: **Two years** is a shock, not a transition.
Governments should talk about **income support** and companies should share their gains.
think: By 2028 the **engineering job** I'm training for might be gone.
Hands-on work may last until about **2031**, but not as a whole career.
do: **Stay** in the degree for now, because the qualification still matters.
Take a **third shift** at the café and save the extra.
feel: **Frightened** and angry that people my age may never get a start.
S2.quote: I'd rather have a bit of money in the bank than a perfect mark, if the jobs are going.
fieldNote: He puts **money** above marks, a sign of how thin his cushion is.
He still sees a **qualification** as worth keeping, a steady and practical view.
Anger is aimed at **government and companies**, not at the technology.

steps.text: Add a third café shift and save the extra
Ask lecturers which engineering roles stay safe longest
Check if a technician route costs less than finishing
Speak up at the students' union about income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to push for the right rules. I'd want a plan for graduates and a basic income pilot. I'd talk about it with my flatmates and raise it at the engineering society.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it would be uncomfortable but manageable. By 2031 I'd have finished, so I'd be applying right as AGI arrives. Robots follow around 2034, so if I choose the physical side of engineering, I'd get a few working years first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and do two placements. I'd move toward something like maintenance or manufacturing engineering, not pure design. I'd also learn how to work with automation systems, since someone has to look after the robots when they arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels pressured but not hopeless. I can see where I'd put my effort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said somebody has to look after the robots. Is that a real job or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. Right now factories need people who set up and fix automated lines. I'm not sure it lasts forever, but it's the best bet I can see for the next decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you fund the extra courses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use short employer-paid ones where I can, and I'd rather not borrow more. If I have to, I'd do them in the evenings and keep the café shifts.

say: Five years gives us time to push for **rules** and a plan for graduates.
I'd raise it with my flatmates and at the **engineering society**.
think: I'd be applying for jobs right as **AGI** arrives, which is uncomfortable.
The **physical** side of engineering would give me a few working years first.
do: Finish the degree and do **two placements** with real firms.
Move toward **maintenance** or manufacturing engineering, not pure design, and learn automation systems.
feel: **Pressured** but not hopeless, since I can see where to put effort.
S3.quote: Right now factories need people who set up and fix automated lines. I'm not sure it lasts forever, but it's the best bet I can see for the next decade.
fieldNote: He turns time into a **specific** aim: maintenance and manufacturing.
He is honest that the **automation job** may not last, which shows steady realism.
He avoids more **borrowing**, a direct result of thin savings.

steps.text: Complete two industry placements before graduating
Choose maintenance and manufacturing modules in third year
Take employer-paid courses on automated production lines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for countries to sort out training and income support, if they decide to. I'd tell younger students that there's no need to quit now. I'd also say that this is why unions and rules still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel okay. By 2036 I'd be 28, with some experience and maybe a decent job, and AI at work might make parts of it easier. The risk comes later, around 2039, when robots do the hands-on work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, get a graduate job in manufacturing, and build up savings for a deposit on a place. I'd learn AI tools at work as they arrive, step by step, since they'd be normal by then. And I'd keep a side skill, maybe teaching evening classes in CAD.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. The long run is cloudy, but I'd have years to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between this one and the 2028 picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time and money. With ten years, I can pay off some loan, find my feet, and move gradually. With two, I'd be forced into a rushed decision with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you in the ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The end point. Even if I'm fine at 28, the same thing is coming at 31 or 32, and I'd want to know what my kids' generation does.

say: Ten years is **plenty** of time to sort out training and income support.
think: By 2036 I'd have **experience** and maybe a decent job.
The real risk comes around **2039**, when robots reach hands-on work.
do: **Finish** the degree and take a manufacturing graduate job.
Build **savings** toward a deposit and teach evening CAD classes.
feel: Mostly **calm**, though the long run is cloudy.
S4.quote: With ten years, I can pay off some loan, find my feet, and move gradually. With two, I'd be forced into a rushed decision with no savings.
fieldNote: **Time and money** explain the change in mood between the fast and slow worlds.
He thinks beyond his own career to his future **children**.
His plan stays **practical**: a graduate job, savings, a side skill.

steps.text: Take a graduate manufacturing job after finishing the degree
Teach evening CAD classes as a side income

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to build savings or retrain. What would help is clear support: a living allowance for students who lose their path, and real training linked to jobs. I'd also want the university to tell us straight which parts of engineering are safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I think should carry the risk. I keep thinking the risk should not sit with eighteen-year-olds on loans while companies take the gains. I'd like them to pay a fair share of the bill.

headlineQuote: I keep thinking the risk should not sit with eighteen-year-olds on loans while companies take the gains.
portrait: Ben is 18 and studies **mechanical engineering**, sharing a cold house and working weekends at a café.
He leans left, wants **rules and support** from firms and government, and aims at hands-on engineering, which changes later.
He is steady rather than bold, **uneasy** in the quiet worlds and alarmed if AGI comes by 2028.
His main pressure is **rent and loans**, and he would hide a shortfall from his dad.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most, because there's no time to save or retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **living allowance** for students who lose their path and training tied to real jobs.
The university being straight about which parts of **engineering** are safe.
